title: AI Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Artificial Intelligence lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: What an AI task looks like
entries.summary: Artificial intelligence, or AI, is a broad area of computing. It includes programs that search for plans or use data to make predictions. Different tasks need different methods.

example.code:
Task: help find a library book
Input: a title typed by a learner
Output: matching titles
Check: compare with the real catalogue

notes: Do not assume an AI label means a program understands everything.

entries.name: Use an explicit rule
entries.summary: A rule tells a program exactly what to do when a condition is met. Some AI systems include rules, while others learn patterns from data.
notes: A rule can only handle the cases its author considered.

entries.name: Represent a problem as states
entries.summary: A state is a description of the current situation. An action changes one state into another. A goal describes the state we want to reach.

example.code:
Start state: at classroom
Action: walk to corridor
Next state: at corridor
Action: walk to library
Goal state: at library

notes: A plan must use moves that are actually allowed in the problem.

entries.name: Store connected places
entries.summary: A graph stores things and their connections. We can describe school rooms with a dictionary whose lists name directly connected rooms.
notes: If travel is allowed both ways, remember to record both connections.

entries.name: Search one step at a time
entries.summary: Breadth-first search checks nearer places before farther places. A queue holds places still waiting to be checked.
notes: Breadth-first search finds fewest moves only when every move has equal cost.

entries.name: A helpful guess can guide search
entries.summary: A heuristic is a useful estimate that guides search. A straight-line distance can suggest which place is nearer, but it may ignore walls or closed paths.

example.code:
Route A: looks short on a map, but a gate is closed
Route B: looks longer, and all paths are open
Next check: verify which moves are allowed

notes: A helpful estimate is not the same as a proven best answer.

entries.name: Respect all constraints
entries.summary: A constraint is a rule every allowed answer must satisfy. A timetable needs a free room and an available teacher at the same time.
notes: An empty answer may mean the rules cannot all be met; do not silently ignore a rule.

entries.name: Rules and learned patterns
entries.summary: A rule-based program follows rules written by people. A learned model finds patterns using examples. Both need testing and can make mistakes.

example.code:
Written rule: a book is long if pages > 200
Learned model: use labelled book examples to choose a pattern
Check: compare decisions with the task definition

notes: Do not call a fixed rule learned unless a learning process actually chose it.

entries.name: Uncertainty deserves a number
entries.summary: Uncertainty means we do not know the outcome for sure. A past fraction can describe observed results, but a small sample gives weak evidence about the future.
notes: Do not turn a small observed fraction into a guaranteed future chance.

entries.name: Agents observe and act
entries.summary: An agent is a system that observes a situation and chooses an action. It needs clear allowed actions and a way to check what happened.

example.code:
Observe: shelf count is zero
Suggest: ask when a book may return
Human checks: is the shelf count current?
Allowed action in this demo: show a suggestion

notes: Giving a system an action tool is different from merely asking it for advice.

entries.name: Check who the data represents
entries.summary: A dataset is a collection of examples. If some groups or situations are missing, a model may work unevenly. Check results for the people and conditions it will serve.

example.code:
Sample: only clear photos in bright daylight
Planned use: photos in daylight and dim rooms
Missing check: results on suitable dim-room examples

notes: Do not assume more examples automatically remove every bias in how data was collected.

entries.name: Keep a person able to review
entries.summary: An AI result should be easy to question and correct. For important choices, people need the evidence, limits and a way to reject a poor suggestion.

example.code:
Suggestion: choose route B
Evidence: route A has a closed gate
Limit: map was checked yesterday
Review: confirm the gate and path are still safe

notes: A fluent explanation can still contain false facts; check the evidence.
